claims.text: Single-phase solid-solution formation in rapidly heated and cooled noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by configurational mixing entropy together with kinetic stabilization.
Extremely fast cooling suppresses atomic diffusion.
Suppressed diffusion during rapid cooling freezes in a mixed state even when thermodynamic driving forces favor phase separation.
Slower cooling allows diffusion-mediated elemental segregation and secondary-phase formation.
The baseline rapid-heating and rapid-quenching process yields a nominally single-phase solid-solution nanoparticle state.
The intervention is a reduced cooling rate after the same rapid-heating pulse used for the baseline.
Cooling rate controls the degree of atomic mobility during cooling.
Fast quenching kinetically locks in a disordered solid solution.
Slower cooling provides sufficient atomic mobility for segregation and phase separation in regions of greater atomic mismatch.
During rapid quenching, high mixing entropy and limited atomic mobility stabilize a metastable homogeneous single phase.
Under slower cooling, differences in atomic size and mixing enthalpy drive phase separation.
Relative to the rapidly quenched baseline, the slowly cooled sample will exhibit secondary-phase diffraction peaks.
Relative to the rapidly quenched baseline, the slowly cooled sample will exhibit increased elemental segregation in TEM/EDX maps.
Slower cooling may alter particle morphology relative to the rapidly quenched baseline.
The proposed behavior applies to compositions having moderate atomic-size mismatch and marginal mixing or segregation driving forces, for which cooling kinetics are consequential.
Systems with extremely favorable mixing or strong segregation tendencies may not follow the proposed cooling-rate response.
